doc.title: Von Freeman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Chicago music scene and family listening
title: His parents' tastes in music and the family record collection
summary: His father liked swing, Guy Lombardo, concert music and Paul Robeson, his mother church music; the flooded record collection is lost.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Oh, they were strictly swingers. Of course my father and mother – see, my mother loved church music. She’s been sanctified all her life. Her mother before her. And my father’s mother was sanctified.
Would she listen to records of church music, too? Or just . . .

At that time they really weren’t recording church music, that music. That really started when they started gospel music. See, because actually the recordings that were made then – there wasn’t but a handful of people recording at that time, to my knowledge.
But they weren’t into Bessie Smith and that kind of thing, blues?
No. My father never was much of a blues person.
Because I know Chicago had a big blues . . .

It’s so strange, and he was stationed on the west side of town, where the blues was. I used to ask him about that. He said, “Blues are fine,” but he was crazy about Guy Lombardo. He’d play all this music. He had these – he’s playing WGN, WBBM, and WMAQ. These were all stations that were playing all of the bands that were coming downtown.
So these were all radio stations, before they became t.v. stations.

Yeah. He said – because I used to ask him. I says, “You dig that?” He says, “Well, you know,” he says, “I’m not one dimensional.” That was one of his words. He said – and he loved concert music, which was kind of rare at that time. But his idol was – out of all of the guys, the idol’s name was this great singer, Paul Robeson. Oh man, he was – when he come to town, everybody went to see him. He had this robust voice, this bass, nobody had heard too much. They heard a lot of baritone singers, but no bass singers. He had a bass voice. And I guess he was someone that they looked up to. So that was – the records that my father liked at that time – and my mother. Her tastes ran right
on along with his – they all liked concert music, what we would call pop music now, and the bands.
Had he ever heard James Reese Europe? Do you remember?

I’ve heard of him, but I never had any records on him, that I can remember. Because I got all of his – well, it doesn’t make any difference now, because the basement used to flood when we first moved here 50 years ago. I had all those records downstairs. One day I looked at them. They were under water and warped. I just dried them off and kept them. But they’re not – they’re unplayable. Because I brought his collection here, because he was so crazy about it. I even had his Victrola box, the box that the Victrola was in.

Yeah, the one without the arm. I kept it for a long – it hasn’t been too long ago that I threw it away, that and my mother’s sewing machine. She had one of the foot pedal sewing machines. I never should have thrown that away, because I haven’t bought a decent electric one since. That thing is so good. You pedal it. But it could really sew. I put it out in – simple – put it out in the alley.
One of them big black ones, heavy iron almost.
Yeah. They’re worth big money now. Some things didn’t get better, you know. Just faster, maybe.
